items.title: Support context-length switches in the hero run
items.body:
Let the hero switch context length mid-run without changing its training schedule. The ladder launcher takes `--seq-len` and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, gate/router weight decay, and `run_progress` therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit `--qk-mult`, applied to all attention layers; `--capacity-factor` overrides the expert receiver capacity.

Harrier now shuffles blocks of 2^20 tokens (`io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len`), which equals the existing 256-sequence block at 4K. At a longer context the outer block permutation stays the same, so only each cell's in-progress 512-block window reorders. With the previous sequence-sized blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T. At 16K the past main-mixture boundary moves from step 108000 to 108096, and a continuation must pass `--accept-mixture-boundary-shift`.

Canonical hero eval stays at 4K packing, so the inherited `eval_dropless/*` series remains comparable, and the first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume. Per-example FLOPs rise with context, so a FLOPs baseline (`--flops-baseline-step`, `--flops-baseline-total`) keeps `throughput/total_gflops` continuous across the handoff. `trigger_hero.sh` records the context, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and boundary acceptance in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record. `launch_diagnostics` gains `--optimizer-tokens-per-step`, `--gate-router-weight-decay`, `--eval-seq-len`, and `--eval-prefix`, so a one-rack rehearsal can use the hero's optimizer settings and report long-context eval separately.

The live run is unchanged. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.

The corrected MuonH d512 treatment completed all **10,980 updates / 1,439,170,560 tokens**.

Idea credit: **Zihan Qiu**.

[d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe_may_compute_opt_mla_hd192_vd256_qc_latentmoe_half_norm_gatednorm_xsa_d768).

[d768](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe-lgr-9110-larry-d768)
(links become available after trainer startup). Validation: lint/type checks
passed; 20 tests passed, one skipped; CPU optimizer-update probe passed.

## Previous attempt (comparison withdrawn)

The earlier September hero-shape treatments completed, but their May references
were not matched controls. Their large loss gap does not establish a causal
regression from gated routing. The unsubmitted H100 ladder rerun is superseded.

<details>
<summary>Historical experiment description and results (superseded)</summary>

## Description

The current EP hero routes the full-width pre-MLP feature `h`; its routed experts receive `RMSNorm(down(h))`. This experiment changes the path to:

```python
u = RMSNorm(h @ W_latent_down)
z = u * sigmoid(silu(u @ W_gate_down) @ W_gate_up)
router_logits = z @ W_router
routed_output = combine(selected_experts(z)) @ W_latent_up
```

The second line is the existing `GatedNorm` class. RMS normalization is a separate operation immediately before that gate. Both the gate and the router read the normalized latent path, and the routed experts receive `z`.

The latent RMSNorm and its learned scale remain trainable. Router gradients flow through the gate, RMSNorm and latent down projection. Router input width changes from hidden width to latent width. Shared experts continue to read `h`; outer norms, QB load balancing, sigmoid combine weights and the shared latent up projection retain the hero behavior.

This tests the combined change of adding the latent gate and routing on its output. It does not separate the contribution of those two changes.

Acknowledgment: **Zihan Qiu proposed this idea.**

User request (verbatim):
> ok准备一个ablation，把latent down之后的norm改成gated norm，然后把router input换成这个gated norm之后的feature，然后follow agent moe ablate一下（acknowledge Zihan Qiu  for the idea in the issue)

Architecture clarification:
> down(h) → RMSNorm → gate → router + experts
>
> 我指的是这个

## Hypothesis or Goal

Routing on the same gated normalized feature consumed by the experts may improve expert specialization and loss enough to offset the gate's runtime cost.

Follow the Agent MoE gates, training only the treatment:

| Gate | Hidden width | Reference FLOP budget | Corrected run ID |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 512 | 3.82e17 | `moe-lgr-9110-d512-rmsgated` |
| 1 | 768 | 2.81e18 | `moe-lgr-9110-d768-rmsgated` |
| 2, conditional | 1024 | 1.16e19 | `moe-lgr-9110-d1024-rmsgated` |
| 2, conditional | 1280 | 3.46e19 | `moe-lgr-9110-d1280-rmsgated` |

Reuse `moe_may_compute_opt_d{dim}_ep1` in `marin-community/marin_moe`. **Do not submit new baseline jobs.** The control implementation exists only for numerical parity tests and analytic schedule calculation.

Gate 1 requires effective speedup above 1 at both small widths. Only then run Gate 2, which requires improvement at all four widths and lower projected loss at 1e21 and 1e23 FLOPs. Use the guide's recentered scaling comparison with exponent 0.0941 and asymptote 1.6.

Record final Paloma macro loss, total tokens, mean throughput over the last 100 training steps, routing statistics, successful Iris completion, W&B `finished` and final checkpoint metadata. Report actual analytic compute and compute-equivalent gain separately from the wall-clock comparison, using each run's own token count and throughput. The historical references use a different recipe and v4-32 hardware; this scaled hero treatment uses v5p-8. Those differences limit attribution of any gain to this intervention.

Prior work: #8105 tested a dynamic latent projection while retaining RMSNorm. It did not test the shared RMSNorm-then-gate routing feature proposed here.

## Status

Both RMSNorm-before-gate runs in the first, small-model experiment stage (Gate 1) completed successfully on September 12: d512 Iris attempt 3 and d768 attempt 2 exited 0, and both W&B runs are finished. Permanent checkpoint metadata is verified at steps 13,642 and 19,378. Routing overflow remained zero and recorded metrics were finite. Source: `edf9b2871`; architecture: `down(h) -> RMSNorm -> gate -> router + routed experts`. Idea: **Zihan Qiu**.

| Hidden width | Treatment Paloma loss | Reference Paloma loss | Tokens, treatment / reference | Last-100 mean tokens/sec, treatment / reference | Treatment non-embedding training FLOPs | Recentered compute ratio | Effective speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 512 | 3.84245491 | 3.54216671 | 1,788,084,224 / 1,439,170,560 | 340,373.87 / 431,263.12 | 3.798955e+17 | 0.217010 | 0.137854 |
| 768 | 3.55822515 | 3.22727251 | 5,079,826,432 / 4,423,680,000 | 200,154.66 / 291,668.98 | 2.798080e+18 | 0.139819 | 0.083556 |

The numerical comparison against historical references is below 1 at both widths, but it is not a matched ablation and cannot establish a gate failure. No d1024/d1280 runs or Gate 2 scaling fit will be launched. No additional baseline or smoke was run.

Using the [Agent MoE guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/experiments/grug/moe/agent.md) scaling-law assumption (loss asymptote 1.6, exponent 0.0941), the compute ratio is `((L_reference - 1.6)/(L_treatment - 1.6))**(1/0.0941)`. Effective speedup is a model-based estimate, not a measured acceleration. It divides the estimated reference time to reach the treatment loss (`compute_ratio * reference_tokens / reference_TPS`) by treatment time (`treatment_tokens / treatment_TPS`). TPS is the mean of exactly the last 100 training steps. These times exclude queueing, preemption, compilation, evaluation and checkpoint overhead. Analytic non-embedding training FLOPs are `3 * (forward_FLOPs_per_token - 2*hidden_dim*vocab_size) * treatment_tokens`; they are distinct from the loss-derived compute ratio.

The reused May references use a different architecture, optimizer/data recipe and v4-32 hardware; treatment uses the [scaled hero latent configuration](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/experiments/grug/moe_latent_gated_router) on v5p-8. This comparison does not isolate the causal effect of adding the gate or changing router input.

- [d512 treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe-lgr-9110-d512-rmsgated) / [reference](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_may_compute_opt_d512_ep1)
- [d768 treatment](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe-lgr-9110-d768-rmsgated) / [reference](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_may_compute_opt_d768_ep1)

Final checkpoints: `gs://marin-us-central1/users/kaiyuew/grug/moe-lgr-9110-d512-rmsgated/dev/checkpoints/step-13642` and `gs://marin-us-central1/users/kaiyuew/grug/moe-lgr-9110-d768-rmsgated/dev/checkpoints/step-19378`.

## Links

- Parent: #4281
- [Implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/experiments/grug/moe_latent_gated_router)
- [Logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/moe-latent-gated-router/.agents/logbooks/moe-latent-gated-router.md)
- [W&B project](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe)
- [Baseline hero code](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d891fba48a7d3729fdac2595df3c6ca292a53b74/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L914)

## Decision Log

- 2026-09-11: Reuse existing Agent MoE baselines, per the user's clarification; run only treatment cells.
- 2026-09-11: Retain latent RMSNorm before the gate, per the user's explicit architecture clarification. Exclude the earlier gate-only interpretation and use fresh `rmsgated` identities.

- 2026-09-11: User instruction: “别smoke浪费卡了，直接跑”. Cancel the pending corrected smoke and directly launch the two full variants.

## Conclusion

### Comparison correction — September 12

The May reference is not a matched control for this ablation. The previous Gate 1 failure wording must not be interpreted as evidence that RMSNorm-then-gate routing hurts quality. The measured losses remain valid for these runs, but the ablation conclusion is inconclusive.

Actual W&B configuration differences include 256/top-4 versus 384/top-8 experts, a full-width MoE versus the hero latent bottleneck, different shared-expert structures, optimizer beta1 0.9062 versus 0.9, minimum LR ratio 0 versus 0.05, different learning rates and token budgets, and training z-loss weight 0 versus 1e-4. Evaluation batch size is 512 in the references versus 32/64 in treatment, with max_eval_batches=8 in both, so the evaluation sample budgets also differ. Hardware is v4-32 versus v5p-8; the estimated speedups do not isolate architectural efficiency.

Tokenizer identity is the same (`meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B`), and named training-source mixture weights agree after removing the treatment's `-llama3` suffix. Cache identity and exact evaluation examples have not been established as equivalent. Different cache paths alone do not prove different source data.

No new runs are being launched. A valid gate ablation needs a reference with the same hero architecture, training recipe, and evaluation protocol, differing only in the intended gate/router intervention. Until such a matched existing reference is found or a new comparison is explicitly agreed, no causal pass/fail conclusion is warranted. Idea credit remains Zihan Qiu.

### Existing baseline search — September 12

Located the hero-shape scaling-ladder references:
- d512: [h100-ladder-d512-ep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824-rno2a](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-ladder-d512-ep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824-rno2a), 16,483,614,720 tokens, batch 1024.
- d768: [h100-ladder-d768-2xep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/h100-ladder-d768-2xep8-bs1024-791tpp-20260824), 47,898,951,680 tokens, batch 1024. A batch-512 sibling also exists.

These share the 384/top-8, hidden/2 latent and expert widths, two shared experts, 6/8 layers, SConv k/attn/mlp, HIST QB with 10k bins, and capacity 1.15 configuration. However, they use the Harrier mixture, top-level Marin tokenizer setting, H100 pooled EP transport, different LR/beta2, and different evaluation budgets. Treatment used the Agent MoE Nemotron/StarCoder/ProofPile recipe with the Llama-3.1 tokenizer setting and batch 32/64 on v5p-8. The ladder's evaluation cache names contain `-llama3`; actual cache-tokenizer equivalence requires further verification, so tokenizer config differences alone should not be interpreted as proven evaluation-token differences.

Completed filtered W&B searches across `marin_moe`, `marin_moe_ragged`, `grug_latent_ablation`, and `qbb_latentmoe_ringEP` for hidden width 512/768, 384 experts, top-8, sequence length 4096, and the treatment's exact top-level tokenizer setting returned only the two treatment runs and the superseded smoke. No matched existing control was found in that scope. Issue #8227 and #8105 baselines use 192/top-4 and are excluded.

The original experiment combined the hero architecture with a different training recipe instead of matching one of these existing hero baselines. To reuse an existing baseline, the treatment must be aligned to its full configuration and schedule. The completed treatment runs cannot currently support a controlled gate comparison. No new training was launched during this search.

items.title: [grug] Apply pending query bias during checkpoint evaluation
items.body:
Apply a checkpoint's `pending_qb_betas` before Grug MoE evaluation callbacks run. A checkpoint-only evaluation at its stop step currently exposes the model parameters and EMA parameters without that pending update. The next normal training forward and the sampling restore path apply the update first, so evaluation can score a different routing state from the one the checkpoint would use on its next forward.

The observed score effect was small on two Hero checkpoints. It was still enough to make the first fixed-policy Paloma comparison semantically incomplete. The original `a1` results are superseded by corrected `a2` runs.

This issue is separate from the router-precision proposal in #8435. The omission occurs regardless of router dot precision. The measured impact comes from checkpoints produced by 20 steps on one B200 rack, so it does not establish the size of the effect for other checkpoints or long runs.

Requested behavior: apply the pending query-bias update to both the current and EMA model views used by evaluation hooks. Ordinary progress, logging, and checkpoint callbacks should continue to use the stored state without launching eager query-bias work.

An experimental fix and regression test exist on Romain's fork, but they have not been merged:

- Initial fix: [`2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/2e392b6c0568e969425eb1bf97b02c853a678860)
- Final scoped fix: [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40)
- Evaluation wrapper: [`train.py`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L679-L693) and [eval-hook application](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1188-L1195)
- Regression test for current and EMA model views: [`test_eval_callback_models_apply_pending_query_bias`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/blob/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40/tests/test_moe_hero_ep.py#L361-L387)

Done when checkpoint evaluation applies the pending query-bias state to current and EMA models, the regression passes, and non-evaluation callbacks avoid this extra work.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Observed behavior

The checkpoint stores `pending_qb_betas` separately from `params`. The training step applies those betas as centered router bias before the next forward, then stores newly computed betas for the following step. The evaluation callback model getters expose raw `params` and EMA parameters. A forced end-of-run callback at an already reached stop step can therefore evaluate the router bias embedded in the parameters and omit the pending update.

The problem appeared while comparing two step-126020 continuation checkpoints under current router arithmetic. Both checkpoints came from the same complete step-126000 native state:

`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-126000`

[`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83) is the observed production source identity for that checkpoint. It does not identify the experimental continuation code.

items.body:
Issue is to describe the Hero Run scaling ladder, config, and track its performance.

Tracking: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/reports/535B-A23B-18T-Token-Hero-Run-Scaling-Ladder--VmlldzoxNzc2MDM5Ng

Details on the full model spec is in the comment below.

### Why run a scaling ladder?

1. This lets us project the model performance and compare it to the scaling projections of our prior recipes. If our projection looks meaningfully worse, then we know we need to go back to the drawing board on some aspect of the model or data. This step can catch a lot of bugs!
2. We can look at how training dynamics change as we scale, in particular the gradient norms and token dropping. In our last run, the scaling ladder caught gradient norm growth to over 4 as we scaled out token horizon, which caused us to find a fix with logit z loss. Later ablations showed that without this fix, runs under certain conditions like high batch size would completely blow up mid-run.
3. We can project our evals across the entire trajectory of the run. This means that across the entire ~100 day run, we know exactly how we are doing compared to the projection. If at any point we fail to match the projection, it can prompt early investigation into training dynamics.
4. If something strange start to happen in the Hero run, we can reference the smaller scales runs to see if its actually normal. For instance, in prior scaling ladders we saw the grad norm grow heavily up to 40% of the run, then decrease as the LR decays. When we saw this on the hero run, having the small scale reference gave us confidence we didn't need to intervene, as long as the gradient followed the same pattern (steady growth for 40% of run).
5. It only costs 1% of total compute.
### What is our EP hardware implementation?
Described in detail here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html.
We are hand-rolling our own EP implementation, props to @ravwojdyla, since we have not found a more performant variant on JAX XLA on GPU. 

### What is our long context extension plan?
Our last run was 8k seqlen pretrain, followed by 65k extension for 1T tokens, followed by 262k extension (to occur end of Aug). Prior to that run we have used 4k seqlen pretrain. For this run we are going back to 4k seqlen pretrain to start, to enable better expert balancing (twice as many sequences per batch). We wanted to minimize risk here because our EP token dropping implementation is more experimental. (our last run was dropless FSDP). Prior tests showed token dropping grow from ~7% to ~40% when extending from 4k to 65k seqlen. Our new pooled/wave EP drops about half as many tokens (3%) at 4k seqlen; however the token dropping is likely still excessively high at 65k seqlen.

We will spend 1-2 days to do an early cooldown at roughly 10-20 days into the run, to enable RL experiments, which will be our first full scale data point at how longer context influences dropping. A nice property of this test is that the cooldown will not contaminate or impact the main run, so we have some flexibility to collect data on how an extension approach impacts dropping. Our options will be:
1. If we have landed a Jax Mixture of Kittens or dropless ragged all-to-all, then we can swap to that for the cooldown. Prior small scale tests showed the model was robust from swapping from small amounts of dropping (5%) to dropless mid-run.
2. Otherwise, we can increase our capacity factor, and accept some amount of dropping.
3. If we find that neither of these options are suitable, the next option would be to introduce sequence level balancing mid-run (though forcing the experts to re-specialize mid-run will likely be worse than accepting some amount of dropping). 

Extending context will involve updating qk_mult according to mscale=X⋅ln(new_seqlen/old_seqlen)+1, testing coefficients near 0.1 (can quickly eval a range during extension on 1 rack). If the data from the first cooldown looks smooth, will plan on 4k->8k at 50 pct into run, then 8k->65k at about 95 pct, then a targeted 262k phase near end, based on data we collect from taking the 67B-A2B from 65k to 262k.

Have further derisked token dropping by staying at 2 shared experts, each at half width. 8 active experts are also at half width. However due to latent MoE 2x compression on active experts, we are effectively running at hidden_dim width neurons shared, and 2x hidden_dim neurons routed. Having 1/3 of our neurons come from shared expert will provide a stronger backbone in the event of high dropping. We see learning still progress with zero loss spikes even at 40 pct dropping.

### What if we see delays, beyond our buffer (hardware failure, MFU degradation)?
Up to roughly 25% of the token budget, the default approach will be to compensate by decreasing the token horizon of the run. Since we are using linear LR decay, we would update the decay rate to still reach 0.05 peak at whatever the new horizon point is, and update the datamix.

items.title: Support context parallelism in the Hero pipeline
items.body:
Add context parallelism to the Hero pipeline mesh, shard attention metadata with query tokens, and form next-token labels before sharding so a context slice can target the first token in the next slice. The smoke runner accepts a context-axis size and calculates batch divisibility without counting context replicas. Update the pipeline environment to CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2, Flash Attention 4 beta 28 or later, and Quack 0.6.4 for SM90 backward.

This draft targets a dependency-only integration branch combining #9119, #9282, and #9279 (which includes #9278). Its five-file diff contains the CP adaptation and dependency update; the prerequisite implementations remain in their existing PRs.

The full 535B, 48-layer model completed ten updates with finite losses on 192 H100s with PP24 × EP4 × CP2, 65,536-token sequences, global batch 96, and 24 microbatches: 6,291,456 tokens per update. Median step time was 68.539 seconds and measured MFU was 9.877%; loss went from 11.792197 to 11.449181. All 24 workers exited successfully. Gate 06 launched c55ab40a29 with exact helper dependency overrides; 3ad8d3ce37 subsequently recorded those dependencies. Runtime and dependency files match 3ad8d3ce37; a later test-only fix compares discontinuous histogram router statistics at matching per-layer execution boundaries. Detailed results are in #9277.

The run still required scratch JAXPP overlays for host-memory mesh rebinding, forward activation-offload placement, and the Dime2 send-buffer lifetime backport. It also retained disposable warmup, host parking of model state, and CUDA synchronization after each step. The required overlays block a stock-install recipe, and the root cause behind the retained synchronization workaround remains unresolved. This is a bounded synthetic-data stepping result.

The integration passed the safe suite with 1,929 tests passed, 5 skipped, and 5 expected failures. After the histogram test fix, all eight affected pipeline tests passed, including the two-CPU CP2-versus-CP1 loss and all-gradient regression. Tolerances are unchanged. Scoped lint passed.

items.title: Experiment: Hero throughput and expert drops at 8K and 16K context
items.body:
Agent-driven experiment issue: the runs and this record were produced by a Claude agent, supervised by @mcwitt.

## TL;DR

On one GB200 NVL72 rack, restoring the hero's step-180000 checkpoint at a fixed 4.19M tokens per step, 8K context trains at 297.0k tokens/s, 1.6% below 4K, and 16K at 292.5k tokens/s, 3.1% below 4K. The fraction of expert assignments dropped rises from 1.9e-4 at 4K to 8.3e-4 at 8K (4.5×) and 2.9e-3 at 16K (16×). The drops come from the receiving shard's per-chunk capacity; the ragged transport counts all of them as `sender_dropped` (see the correction comment). Each arm has three seeds; the seed-to-seed standard deviation is at most 0.03 MFU points and 4% to 7% of the drop fraction.

## Description

The hero plan in #8435 moves from 4K to 8K sequences at 50% of training (step ~195k) and to 65K at ~95%. These runs measure what the 8K switch costs in throughput and expert-capacity drops before it happens, with 16K as the next point and a 4K control from the same checkpoint.

Setup:

* Source: `main` at f38da1173de79f1eacd5f54bcfb88db6cb0a9f6e with no code changes. Launcher: `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py`.
* Checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000`, the newest permanent hero checkpoint on 2026-09-30. The current hero run id records that it started from step 146k.
* Hardware and parallelism: one rack (16 nodes × 4 GB200), EP64, the hero's ragged all-to-all transport and capacity factor 1.15.
* Every arm keeps 4,194,304 tokens per step (65,536 per GPU), so the learning rate from the hero's heuristic (`MoeHeuristic` in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/heuristic.py`, which scales with tokens per step and total tokens) is the same in all arms. `--schedule-steps 390251` is the hero's full schedule length, so the restored step sits at the hero's position in the learning-rate schedule.
* `qk_mult`, the multiplier on the query-key attention scale, follows the #8435 extension rule `1.3 × (0.1 × ln(seq / 4096) + 1)`.
* Each run trains steps 180000 to 180099 with the production watch interval (10) and coordinated GC interval (100). There is no eval and no checkpoint write.
* The trainer seed sets the data shuffle, so seeds 0, 1, and 2 train on different batches.
* Statistics cover steps 180010 to 180099 (90 steps). Each run contributes its median MFU, median tokens/s, and mean drop fraction; the tables report mean ± standard deviation across the three seeds. Starting the window at step 180030 instead moves no run's median MFU by more than 0.03 points.

| Arm | `--seq-len` | `--batch-size` | `--qk-mult` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K control | 4096 | 1024 | 1.3 |
| 8K | 8192 | 512 | 1.39 |
| 16K | 16384 | 256 | 1.48 |

Command for one run (8K, seed 0):

```bash
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_diagnostics \
  --run-id mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930 --seed 0 \
  --num-steps 180100 --schedule-steps 390251 \
  --batch-size 512 --seq-len 8192 --qk-mult 1.39 --gc-interval 100 \
  --restore-from s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-180000 \
  --version dev --run
```

## Results

| Arm | tokens/s | vs 4K | step time | MFU | drop fraction | vs 4K |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 4K | 301.9k ± 0.2k | | 13.89 s | 28.25 ± 0.02% | 1.86e-4 ± 0.08e-4 | 1× |
| 8K | 297.0k ± 0.2k | −1.6% | 14.12 s | 28.47 ± 0.02% | 8.29e-4 ± 0.39e-4 | 4.5× |
| 16K | 292.5k ± 0.3k | −3.1% | 14.34 s | 29.37 ± 0.03% | 2.94e-3 ± 0.20e-3 | 16× |

The logged `moe/receiver_drop_fraction` is zero in every run because the ragged transport hard-codes it to zero and counts receiver-capacity clipping as `sender_dropped`. Peak HBM was 103.1 GiB per GPU in every run. In every run, including the 4K control, the mean drop fraction over steps 180055 to 180099 was 0.75 to 1.00 times the mean over steps 180010 to 180054, so part of the measured drop fraction may be a transient after restore.

The live hero (11 racks, 4K) measured over steps 183310 to 183710 on 2026-09-30 had a median MFU of 26.47% and a mean drop fraction of 9.1e-5.

Caveats:

* MFU uses the analytic FLOP count, which charges more attention FLOPs per token at longer sequences (full causal attention on every fourth layer, a 2048-token window elsewhere). MFU therefore rises with sequence length while tokens/s falls. Compare arms by tokens/s.
* The one-rack 4K drop fraction is about 2× the 11-rack hero's. We have not tested the cause. The ratios between arms are the quantity to carry to the hero; an 8K hero drop fraction near 4e-4 is an extrapolation from that ratio, not a measurement.
* Each run covers 100 steps after the switch. Routing over thousands of steps at the new length is untested.
* The 8K and 16K arms change `qk_mult` together with sequence length.
* The diagnostic's peak learning rate comes from a one-rack token budget and is 0.69× the hero's. The diagnostic also leaves the attn_gate/router weight decay at 0 (the hero uses 0.02). Loss values are not comparable with the hero's.
* At 8K and 16K, XLA logged at compile time that rematerialization could only reduce its memory estimate to 193 GiB against a 161 GiB limit. The warning does not stop compilation. The runs trained normally with a runtime peak HBM of 103.1 GiB, the same as 4K, so the estimate overstated actual use.

## Links

* W&B runs (project `marin_moe`, group `moe-hero-ep`): 4K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx4k-s2-20260930); 8K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx8k-s2-20260930); 16K [s0](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s0-20260930), [s1](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s1-20260930), [s2](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mhep-ctx16k-s2-20260930)
* Hero plan: #8435. 262K context-parallel probe on the same hardware: #8754.

## Conclusion

At the planned 4K to 8K switch, expect about 1.6% fewer tokens per second and about 4.5× the 4K drop fraction, still below 0.1% of assignments on one rack. At 16K the costs are 3.1% and 16×.

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This campaign tested whether the ragged EP64 all-to-all path could match the fixed-transport hero throughput target while keeping trained-router drops below 2% at the full 8/384 hero shape on one NVL72 rack. The drop criterion is met with large margin: the real-LR drop-trajectory run averaged 0.107% drops over steps 250-299 at cf 1.15. Throughput improved from the initial 20.20% MFU / 223k tok/s configuration to a 21.82% MFU / 241k tok/s frontier after QuACK GEMM scheduling work, with zero drops and bit-identical loss across the tuning arms. The issue's current conclusion is that the in-scope configuration and compute-tuning levers are exhausted: split counts, store width, symmetric buffers, fused device kernel, command buffers, HBM optimizer residency, GEMM tile/cluster/persistence, backward mask removal, and overlap-limit changes do not close the remaining gap. Reaching the original ~25% / ~300k tok/s target now depends on a faster structural transport path, tracked separately in marin-ep, rather than more launch-flag tuning here.

### Helpful links
- Prior ragged EP64 crash/fix campaign: #8077
- Capacity/drop analysis: #8062
- Upstream ragged all-to-all gate: https://github.com/openxla/xla/issues/47283
- Configuration phase conclusion: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5305649465
- Compute-tuning frontier: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5308322722
- Final in-scope lever closure: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8317#issuecomment-5309167198
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## TL;DR

Campaign start. The ragged all-to-all hero (E384, top-8, i3072, EP64 on one NVL72 rack) runs at 20.20% MFU / 223k tokens/s (`ra2a-mw-g17`, cf 1.00, LR≈0 harness). The goal is throughput comparable to the fixed-transport `moe_hero_ep` template (~25% MFU, ~300k tokens/s per rack) while holding steady-state trained-router drops under 2%.

## Description

#8077 root-caused and fixed the EP64 one-shot crash (openxla/xla#47283, kMaxPeers rebuild wheel) and validated the first ragged EP64 hero run. The ragged transport pools receiver capacity per device, so it drops far less than `fixed_all_to_all` at the same capacity factor: at cf 1.1–1.2 the trained-regime drop rate measures ≤0.05% (analytical replay of #8062 histograms; empirical r02 at EP16), versus ~4% for the fixed template at cf 1.30–1.33. What remains is a throughput gap.

Reference points at hero scale on one rack: fixed transport at iso-active-compute (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-i6144-cf133-fp32-20260814-c`) reaches 23.6% MFU / 251k tokens/s at ~3.9% drops; the half-active-compute reference (`mhep-baseline-e192k4-cf133-fp32-20260814-b`, i3072) reaches 25.3% / 346k.

Constraints: no model change, and no quantization beyond what `moe_hero_ep` on main already performs (per the [fidelity discussion](https://openathena.slack.com/archives/C0AHF5KV11Q/p1786740832465729?thread_ts=1786583521.652629&cid=C0AHF5KV11Q)). The ragged training path is currently bf16 end to end.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reach ~25% MFU / ~300k tokens/s at the full hero shape (d6144/L48, E384, top-8, i3072, latent 3072, batch 1024) on one NVL72 rack with the ragged transport, then demonstrate <2% steady-state drops at the chosen capacity posture and loss parity against the existing EP implementation via `small_scale_abl_launch.py`.

## Status

h01 (cf 1.15 posture baseline) and h02 (latency-hiding scheduler + overlap limit 4, retesting the safe-flag retreat adopted on the broken barrier generation) are running. Queued: splits-per-peer sweep at EP64, command buffers at the #8277 capture set, XProf anatomy of the best configuration.

items.body:
Benchmark the BF16 kernels and fusions in [OLMo-core 3](https://allenai.org/papers/olmocore3) against Marin's current Grug MoE path to find small changes that improve training throughput. Start with candidates that preserve the current BF16 precision, routing, and optimizer behavior. MXFP8 training adoption remains deferred over stability concerns.

Use OLMo-core revision [`a800c06`](https://github.com/allenai/olmo-core/tree/a800c06edcec8e4652de2f80fe0ea572d689fcc3) as the source reference. Use the resolved [GB200 Hero recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/hero_recipe.py) to define baseline shapes and settings. Profile and rank:

- Grouped expert GEMMs: compare forward, activation-gradient, and weight-gradient legs on GB200 at Hero's actual latent dimensions, rows per expert, and uneven group sizes. Include the complete expert MLP forward/backward boundary and any conversion or layout costs.
- Activation, weighting, and buffer fusions: inspect SwiGLU forward/backward, route-weight application, and dispatch/combine staging copies. Benchmark opportunities that remove an intermediate allocation or memory pass after checking what our current kernels already fuse.
- Shared-expert compute packing: compare the current separate shared MLP calls with packed projections or grouped launches while preserving separate logical parameter matrices and MuonH update semantics.

Reuse [bench_grouped_wgrad.py](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_grouped_wgrad.py) and [Hero diagnostics](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/2ae9115497494655baac21dd03a61d205ac73ab2/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_diagnostics.py). Related work: #9077 (XLA/cuDNN ragged-dot replacement), #8311 (fused EP backend). Link existing results and avoid repeating covered comparisons without a new candidate or changed configuration.

Done when:

- Record pinned source/dependency versions, hardware, shapes, routing/group counts, warmup, timing boundary, repeated timings, and numerical comparisons for each candidate. Reuse identical seeded normal or checkpoint-derived operands across matched variants; include the operand seed or checkpoint in the recorded configuration.
- Separate kernel time, complete operator time, peak memory, and full training-step time. For any overlap candidate, compare an unsplit batch, sequential chunks, and chunks with communication overlapped against expert compute.
- Validate promising candidates in a bounded Hero-shaped run on the same hardware, checkpoint, batches, token-to-expert assignments after capacity filtering, precision, and optimizer as the control. Report forward/backward agreement, loss, dropped-assignment counts, memory, and throughput, including integration overhead.
- Publish a ranked adopt/defer/reject recommendation here, with commands and result/profile links. An outcome with no useful speedups is valid. Keep changes that alter the numerical recipe, including MXFP8, as separately evaluated follow-ups.

items.title: [grug] Raise hero single-rack MFU from 28.2% to 31.1%
items.body:
On one GB200 NVL72 rack, these commits shorten the `moe_hero_ep` training step from 13.90 to 12.61 s (28.24% to 31.13% MFU), with loss inside the run-to-run noise of unchanged code. The last commit adds a PGLE profile builder; with a profile built from the program's own trace, the step is 12.52 s (31.37% MFU). The changes come from two campaigns: the first worked down the step's most expensive scopes, and the second benchmarked OLMo-core 3's BF16 MoE kernels against this path (#9636) and kept the leads that paid.

Each row is one single-rack run (`cw-us-east-08a`, 64 GPUs) restored from `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` step 180000, seed 0, 100 steps, on main's production PJRT wheel with the code's defaults. The time is the median step duration over steps 180011-180099 without the three profiled steps, and the gain is the previous row's time divided by this row's, minus one. Repeated runs of the same code differ by about 0.1%. The runs used trees from before a final round of refactors and review fixes (types, helpers, comments, tests, and code paths the hero does not take); the hero's train step lowers to the same program at these commits.

| Change | Commit | s/step | MFU | Gain |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | b4d1761ff2 | 13.899 | 28.24% | |
| Remat discounts the host-offloaded carry | 13448300c6 | 13.737 | 28.57% | +1.18% |
| Unfilled ragged transport buffers | a544f2571c | 13.542 | 28.99% | +1.44% |
| Expert-side routing-weight gradient | 9ea5098c10 | 13.130 | 29.90% | +3.14% |
| Streaming Triton short convolution | 98412f4efc | 13.059 | 30.06% | +0.55% |
| SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM epilogue | 50e50512a5 | 12.943 | 30.33% | +0.89% |
| Device-side kernel availability check | 1f08c52720 | | | no hero change |
| Triton router top-k | 42fc5766b3 | 12.875 | 30.49% | +0.53% |
| Token-major dispatch scatter | 0ba2cb6bbd | 12.730 | 30.83% | +1.14% |
| Shared and chunk GEMMs under the MoE transports | 45c2459f70 | 12.638 | 31.06% | +0.73% |
| Synchronous collectives without the carry offload | 8fd3af2759 | | | no hero change |
| Shared-expert SwiGLU in QuACK epilogues | ffecc63a46 | 12.652 | 31.03% | -0.11% |
| No routed pre-activation store under remat | 9ce3cfc1a4 | 12.611 | 31.13% | +0.33% |
| PGLE profile builder, run with a profile | daa46e2be5 | 12.515 | 31.37% | +0.77% |

The scheduling row groups three changes that do not stand alone. The MLP-section weight prefetch (from #9481) lets the first shared expert's gate/up projection run beside the first ragged dispatch, but it also moves a weight slice behind each layer's carry offload copy on the same memcpy stream, which stalls the forward for 98-152 ms/step on the production wheel. The barrier that issues the slices before the carry copy removes that stall, and costs 0.49% on a program that does not collide; at the end of the series, disabling it alone slows the step by 0.79%. The shared-expert QuACK row is negative because, after the scheduling row, the shared GEMMs are what covers the transports: the 0.18 s/step of compute it saves left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Removing it from the end of the series still slows the step, by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs, so it stays.

Changes whose gain was below about 0.3% were removed from the final tip one at a time and kept only if the tip slowed by more than 0.2% without them; a result between 0.2% and 0.4% got a second pair. That dropped a scatter-based inverse permutation (the tip was 0.04% faster without it) and a Triton bincount (0.22% and 0.10%), and kept the routed pre-activation change (0.47%) and the shared-expert QuACK change. The four rows from the unfilled transport buffers through the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward were measured with the inverse permutation in their base and before a behavior-neutral review cleanup; without it, the last of them ran the same 12.943 s.

Numerics: the unfilled transport buffers, the top-k kernel, the dispatch scatter and the pre-activation change are bitwise. The routing-weight gradient, the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward and the short convolution's weight gradient change at bf16 rounding; the shared-expert SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator, so the forward changes at rounding level and 0.06-0.3% of routing assignments differ downstream, as close to an fp32 reference as before; the carry barrier moves fusion boundaries. On the ragged backend, an accepted assignment whose combine weight is zero, or small enough for `w * dout` to underflow, gets a zero combine-weight gradient rather than `<dout, y>`, which `moe_mlp` documents; sigmoid and softmax routers produce such weights only by underflow, where their logit gradient is as small. Against main over 100 steps, the final tip's loss differs by at most 3.8e-4 (2.6e-4 with the profile), against 3.3e-4 between two runs of main. Four of about 30 runs took a late upward excursion of about 1e-3 that value-identical variants also showed, so it is run-to-run nondeterminism.

Peak HBM rises from 103.1 to 123.2 GiB of a 143.75 GiB pool, mainly the 18 GiB routed MoE output that the expert-side routing-weight gradient saves; under the carry offload the launcher defaults to `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.78` and slop 105, validated on one rack only. A ragged run without the carry offload keeps XLA's default scheduler, which ignores the one-in-flight collective limit, so that configuration now runs collectives synchronously; the hero always offloads and is unaffected. PGLE needs a profile built from a trace of the exact program and mesh, so the production run needs its own before it gains the last row; automatic PGLE stays off. The memcpy-stream collision is avoided per program here; the patched PJRT wheel that gives host transfers their own streams is left for a follow-up.

This supersedes #9481: it carries that PR's mirror transpose parameters, weight prefetch and PGLE builder, and replaces its two-stage chunk pipelining with the dispatch overlap above, which with PGLE measured 12.666 s/step against 12.783 for pipelining with PGLE, the latter on a patched PJRT wheel without the copy stall (both before the kernels above and the shared-expert change). Part of #9636; the OLMo-core comparison and its adopt/defer/reject table are on that issue. Research records: `.agents/logbooks/mfu30.md` and `.agents/logbooks/olmo9636.md` on `research/mcwitt/mfu30`.

items.title: Experiment: Marin EP fused expert-parallel MoE backend for the GB200 hero (EP64)

labels.name: tldr
labels.description: Issue has a community-friendly TL;DR summary

items.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

Marin EP is an experimental Grug MoE backend for the GB200 hero: group-pooled waterfilling acceptance plus fused Mosaic-GPU transport, now working multi-process in the production 1-process/GPU topology. Upstream replaced NVSHMEM with the NCCL device API via collective metadata; with a patched PJRT wheel (kMaxPeers-128 + two 4096-alignment fixes), `--xla_gpu_enable_dynamic_slice_fusion=false`, and a separate collective allocator, the fused transport trains conformantly across nodes. The current EP64 hero best is 17.0 s/step, ~247k tokens/s/rack (~22.6% MFU) at 0.5-0.6% drops — from 18.1 s at the start of the campaign — via fused transport (17.75), Pallas Blackwell ragged-dot expert GEMMs (17.08, ~1.6x the QuACK/cuDNN path), and per-leg kernel configs (17.0). A correctness bug was found on the way: the cuDNN grouped Wgrad silently miscomputes unless group offsets are 64-aligned (#8339, fixed on the measurement branch). Profiles show the remaining 5 s to the 25% / 350k gate sits in attention/dense GEMMs, XLA fusion mass, and FSDP one-shot collectives rather than the MoE path.

### Helpful links
- Latest EP64 ladder + profile: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311#issuecomment-5309381342 and https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311#issuecomment-5309484707
- Multi-process transport unblock (three XLA findings + fixes): https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8311#issuecomment-5308550100
- Wgrad correctness bug: #8339; barrier-bound context: #8077, #8313, openxla/xla#47283
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

Experimental fused expert-parallel MoE backend for `moe_hero_ep` (d6144, 192 latent experts, top-4, EP64 on GB200 NVL72), developed simulator-first against a dense oracle: behavior spec, NumPy oracle, message-passing correctness simulator with explicit backward, and L0/L1 performance models before hardware. The backend lives in `levanter.grug._moe.ep_marin` (+ `marin_ep_transport`); spec and research artifacts under `experiments/marin_ep/`. Branch `marin-ep`. This is an experimental backend: it has not run a full-scale training gate and is not a production default.

Differences from `fixed_all_to_all`/`ragged_all_to_all`:

- Acceptance is deterministic group-pooled waterfilling over global expert counts, pooling capacity across each owner's co-located experts. It is EP-degree invariant and drops 0.31% at cf 1.33 under hero-calibrated skew, vs ~4% for the per-cell rule at the same buffer bytes.
- Transport is one generic Mosaic-GPU put kernel (`put_segments`) that writes each owner's expert-major receive pool directly, eliminating both local permutes; dispatch and combine plans are transposes of each other, so the backward runs the same kernel with the opposite plan (custom_vjp).

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reach >= 25% MFU and >= 350k tokens/s/rack at the hero shape with EP64, keeping drops < 2% in the trained-router regime. Baseline `fixed_all_to_all`: 24.04% MFU, 262,683 tok/s at cf 1.30 with 3.96% drops.

## Status

- Multi-process fused transport validated end-to-end: 8-rank cross-node conformance (values, drops bit-identical to the ragged path, all gradients at the bf16 floor), then EP16 proxy (17.0 s vs 18.05 flat) and EP64 hero. Requires the patched PJRT wheel `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/research/mcwitt-ra2a/pjrt-kmax128-align4096-dev0811-20260816/` and `--xla_gpu_enable_dynamic_slice_fusion=false`; an upstream report of the three XLA findings is drafted pending review.
- EP64 hero ladder (25-step runs, same wheel/flags, single draws +/-2pp): brd 17.0 s/step (~247k tok/s, ~22.6% MFU, 0.5-0.6% drops) < mgpu-cute 17.75 < flat ragged 18.0. Flavors `ep-marin-mgpu-brd` / `ep-marin-mgpu-cudnn-cute` on branch `marin-ep-8081`.
- Expert GEMMs now run on jax's Pallas Blackwell ragged-dot kernel (fwd + dgrad; 1195-1531 TF/s per leg at true hero shapes, ~1.6x the QuACK/cuDNN path) with the 64-alignment-fixed cuDNN grouped wgrad (#8339). Hero dims need N-padding to the collective tile (2I=6272, I=3136).
- Dead ends recorded: PGLE OOMs on the fused flavor (its profiling pass falls back to dense a2a); command buffers neutral; scoped ragged groups and the hierarchical two-hop transport slower than flat; a memory-bound fused consumer hides only ~7% (M7a) — expert-major send order is the overlap lever, and M7b targets gating the ragged-dot group scheduler on arrival flags.
- Remaining gap to 25% MFU / 350k tok/s: ~5 s/step in attention/dense GEMMs (4.9 s busy), XLA fusions (3.5 s), and FSDP one-shot collectives (2.8 s + 1.05 s barriers) — outside the EP transport scope; fp8 wire + attention/fusion work are the ranked candidates.

## Links

* Logbook: `.agents/logbooks/marin-ep.md` (entries MEP-001..MEP-044; measurement branch `marin-ep-8081`, PR branch `marin-ep` / #8320)
* Plan: `.agents/projects/20260814_marin_ep_kernel.md`; M7 plan: `.agents/projects/marin-ep-m7.md`; spec: `experiments/marin_ep/SPEC.md`
* W&B: marin-community/marin_moe (runs `mep-*-20260815/16`)

## Decision Log

- 2026-08-14: adopted group-pooled waterfilling (pool group = experts per device) into the spec; per-cell and per-expert pooling both leave ~4% drops at cf 1.33.
- 2026-08-14: transport substrate = Pallas Mosaic-GPU remote puts + arrival semaphores (584 GB/s/device untuned on one tray, zero custom CUDA).
- 2026-08-15: multi-controller runs fall back to ragged transport after pinning the upstream NVSHMEM removal; hierarchical transport is the planned successor.

- 2026-08-16: multi-process fused transport adopted (collective metadata + patched wheel + dynamic-slice-fusion off) after the NVSHMEM-removal block proved obsolete; hierarchical transport retired.
- 2026-08-16: expert activation-path GEMMs moved to jax's Pallas Blackwell ragged-dot kernel; cuDNN grouped wgrad kept with the 64-alignment fix (#8339).

## Conclusion

items.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
items.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. items.title: [experiment] Hero 535B at 65K on H100: 15.5% MFU with PP24/EP8
items.body:
## TL;DR

The full 535B, 48-layer Hero model completed ten finite synthetic updates at sequence length 65,536 on 192 H100s with **15.523% median MFU and 174.432 seconds per step**. The working recipe is standard 1F1B, PP24/EP8, batch 384 (48 pipeline microbatches), BF16 MuonH, and host activation/optimizer offload. Keep batch 384 as the best measured throughput recipe; CP2 provides the validated batch 96 alternative. Stop DualPipeV performance exploration for now. DualPipeV also completed ten updates, but required extra recomputation, cotangent offload, and task waits and reached only 4.917% MFU.

CP2 also completed ten full-model updates with finite losses at **batch 96 (6Mi tokens), 9.877% MFU and 68.539 seconds/update**, with all 24 workers exiting successfully. This uses PP24/EP4/CP2: each GPU handles 32K tokens of each 65K sequence. The earlier 15.523% result uses batch 384 (24Mi tokens), so these are different throughput/batch tradeoffs.

Here Mi means 2^20 tokens. These are bounded systems diagnostics from fresh initialization with synthetic data. Production checkpoint continuation, long-run stability, and training quality remain unvalidated. No production GB200 run was changed.

## Description

Adapted `experiments/grug/moe_pipeline/pipeline.py` to Hero's actual blocks, preserving the model shape, latent/shared experts, SConv, absolute local/global attention schedule, and QB router updates. The full model has 535,477,106,688 parameters, 48 layers, width 6144, 384 routed experts, top-8 routing, and latent/expert intermediate width 3072. FA4 (`gpu_fa4_cute`) is active. No FP8 was needed.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Establish a memory-safe H100 recipe for the existing Hero shape at 32K and 65K, then improve utilization by filling the pipeline without changing the core model.

## Status

### Validated 65K 1F1B scaling

All rows use the full model, 192 H100s on `cw-rno2a`, PP24/EP8, one process per eight-GPU node, six expert transport waves, BF16 MuonH, both host offloads, and explicit device completion after each update. Every row completed ten finite updates with all 24 workers exiting successfully.

| Microbatches | Global batch | Median seconds/step | Median MFU | Run |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| 8 | 64 | 64.626 | 6.983% | [m8](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m8-sync-20260918-19) |
| 16 | 128 | 86.743 | 10.405% | [m16](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m16-sync-20260918-21) |
| 24 | 192 | 108.584 | 12.468% | [m24](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m24-sync-20260918-22) |
| 32 | 256 | 130.207 | 13.864% | [m32](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m32-sync-20260918-23) |
| 48 | 384 | 174.432 | 15.523% | [m48](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-1f1b-ep8-65k-full-m48-sync-20260918-24) |

The maximum standard-1F1B activation backlog caps at 24 microbatches. Increasing batch beyond m24 improved pipeline occupancy without increasing that maximum backlog. The m48 final loss was 11.62364388. The reported step timer excludes some global loss collection/inter-step overhead; these comparisons use the same timer and model FLOP accounting.

Earlier full-model milestones: 32K completed three updates at batch 8 (~18.84 seconds, ~1.28% MFU); 65K batch 8 completed ten (~65.69 seconds, ~0.859%). Short-context DualPipeV reached ~13.91% median MFU with AdamW and ~13.72% with MuonH; those are different batch/context recipes and do not establish long-context superiority.

### H100 context parallelism: smaller global batch

[Full CP2 run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-cp2-full-65k-20260919-06) preserved the 535B/48-layer model and 65,536-token sequences on the same 192 H100s. It used PP24/EP4/CP2, 24 pipeline microbatches, global batch 96, BF16 MuonH, six expert waves, both host offloads, and the existing per-update device-completion workaround. Ten losses were finite (11.792197 → 11.449181); all 24 Iris and native exits were zero.

| Configuration | Pipeline microbatches | Global batch | Tokens/update | Median seconds/update | Median MFU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| PP24/EP8/CP1 | 24 | 192 | 12Mi | 108.584 | 12.468% |
| PP24/EP4/CP2 | 24 | 96 | 6Mi | 68.539 | 9.877% |
| PP24/EP8/CP1, best throughput | 48 | 384 | 24Mi | 174.432 | 15.523% |

CP2 halves sequence length per GPU to 32K and global microbatch from eight sequences to four. With the same PP24 topology and 24 pipeline microbatches, it halves tokens/update; reducing microbatch count from the previous best's 48 to 24 reduces total batch by another factor of two. CP2 processes fewer tokens per update and has a shorter measured update time, at lower token throughput. The step timer excludes some global loss collection/inter-step overhead. The runs also use different FlashAttention/CuTe helper versions, so this is not an isolated CP-only speed comparison.

Validation before the full run:

- Three two-H100 CP2-versus-CP1 BF16 attention cases passed: causal, sliding window 2048, and packed/padded sequences. Outputs matched exactly; maximum absolute dQ error was 0.0004883 and dK/dV error was 0.03125 with absolute and relative tolerances both 0.07. Native SM90 support is in #9282, based on #9117.
- A five-layer, width-8, six-token CPU model matched CP2 pipeline versus CP1 unsplit-model loss and all parameter gradients with absolute and relative tolerances both 1e-5, including packed boundaries, SConv and activation offload. The next-token label shift requires gathering token IDs across CP before shifting; hidden activations remain sequence-sharded.
- Two full-width blocks at 65K passed repeated gradient and host-state MuonH updates on eight H100s. An eight-layer PP4/EP4/CP2 pipeline then passed ten updates on 32 H100s.
- The pipeline environment initially selected FA4 b16, which lacks `AuxData`. The validated CP stack uses FA4 b28, CUTLASS DSL 4.6.2 and Quack 0.6.4 while retaining JAX/JAXlib 0.11.0 for JAXPP.

CP2 launch source: `c55ab40a29c4bda8d1ed54c7e31ddbbbff209e8f`, combining the open CP stack through #9119, #9282, and the Hero pipeline adapter. The full run used the same scratch JAXPP/Dime2 overlays as the successful smaller gate, plus the explicit helper versions above. The launcher applied the helper versions above during setup; the equivalent dependency declarations were subsequently recorded locally in `3ad8d3ce37ded02c956d9811865119f8f189c71e`; the five-file CP integration and dependency update are published in draft #9283 above a dependency-only base combining #9119, #9282 and #9279. The draft still requires the scratch runtime fixes described below. Evidence: `cp2-full-65k06-evidence.json`, `cp2-pp4-65k05-evidence.json`, `cp-fullwidth65k-muon04-evidence.json` and `cp-sm90-parity02-evidence.json` under `scratch/hero-h100-20260916/`.

### Memory and correctness findings

- JAXPP mesh rebinding failed to preserve Host/Device memory targets: minimal reproduction in [NVIDIA/jaxpp#13](https://github.com/NVIDIA/jaxpp/issues/13).
- Forward partitioning moved activation D2H copies into backward. Keeping copies in forward and preserving pinned-host intermediate shardings saved exactly **12 GiB/device** at eight outstanding microbatches in the 24-layer diagnostic (first-backward live memory 26.10 → 14.10 GiB). CPU actual-partition value/gradient tests and GPU host ABI checks passed.
- Embedding recomputation reduced stage-zero activation retention. Parking real state on host during disposable warmup avoids holding real and warmup model copies on GPU together.
- The working allocator settings are `cuda_async`, memory fraction 0.91, preallocation false. BFC trials encountered large-allocation failures despite aggregate free space. Raising preallocation to 0.95 also caused an NCCL allocation failure.
- Two unsynchronized full m8 runs produced NaNs at updates 10 and 8. Finite-state instrumentation passed, and explicit completion of all eight local GPUs after each update passed repeatedly. This supports a timing association; **the race/root cause is unresolved**. Small fixed-weight host-lifetime and receive-buffer-reuse probes passed and did not reproduce the failure.
- The Dime2 send-capsule lifetime fix is already available in [upstream 78458f8](https://github.com/NVIDIA/jaxpp/commit/78458f8b258f0fd467be13b4b8e7056a853e320b). The diagnostic stack backports it; this is not a new upstream contribution.

### DualPipeV negative results

Full topology: 48 logical / 24 physical stages, EP8, 48 microbatches, batch 384, same 65K context and model.

- Splitting activation and weight backward generated ~13.24 GiB of retained device intermediates per delayed weight backward. Independent recomputation removed those residuals but added compute.
- Offloading original delayed cotangents removed another memory constraint. Full warmup then passed, but asynchronous real execution OOM'd in `bwdA_40` on the first update. Free-memory counters printed after failure do not prove fragmentation.
- Waiting for each task's outputs completed ten updates: [full35](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-dualpipe-ep8-65k-full-taskwait-20260919-35), 565.108 seconds, 4.791% MFU.
- Waiting only around backward tasks also completed ten, all 24 native exits zero: [full37](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-dualpipe-ep8-65k-full-bwdwait-20260919-37), 550.704 seconds, 4.917% MFU, final loss 11.62360668. Only ~2.5% faster. Diagnostic memory logging remained enabled; its overhead and recomputation/transfer costs were not separately measured.
- Eight expert waves regressed the eight-layer diagnostic: 55.17 vs 46.52 seconds, recorded peak 68.97 vs 67.27 GiB. Rejected.

## Links

- Related GB200 EP investigation: #7279.
- Runtime incident record: https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/445
- Original CP1 source base: `96da2a6cdce401187239846957687fdde22cf8a5`; JAXPP pin used for overlays: `46b8443eed01f54688dd24ae451203a504b1cff8`.
- Local evidence/manifests: `scratch/hero-h100-20260916/`, especially `full65k-m48-sync24-evidence.json`, `dual65k-full-taskwait35-evidence.json`, and `dual65k-full-bwdwait37-evidence.json`. These ignored workspace artifacts are not a published reproduction package. W&B links above retain the run evidence.

## Decision Log

- Preserve core Hero shape; use BF16 and MuonH with both offloads; no FP8 required.
- Keep 1F1B at 65K/batch384 as the working result. End further DualPipeV throughput sweeps and prepare reviewable changes.
- Build on the existing open CP stack (#9116–#9119), as authorized; port its native attention backward to SM90. CP2 now validates the full model at batch96/6Mi tokens. No competing CP implementation was introduced.

## Conclusion

15.523% MFU establishes bounded full-model 65K feasibility on H100s at batch384/24Mi tokens. CP2 establishes a smaller batch96/6Mi alternative at 9.877% MFU. Prepare separate changes for (1) the small Muon expert-stack sharding fix and regression, (2) upstream JAXPP memory-space and forward-host-residual correctness fixes, and (3) the Hero pipeline adapter, runner, tests, and documented recipe. Treat startup warmup APIs as a separate dependency and keep DualPipeV-only overlays/telemetry out of the minimal 1F1B stack. A clean dependency pin and reproducible launcher still need to replace the scratch overlays before claiming stock-install reproduction. Retain the step-completion workaround until its underlying timing issue is understood.

items.title: Support context-length switches in the hero run
items.body:
Let the hero switch context length mid-run without changing its training schedule. The ladder launcher takes `--seq-len` and holds 4,194,304 tokens per rack per update, so the sequence batch shrinks as the context grows (2816 sequences at 16K on 11 racks). The step count (390251), learning rates, decay, gate/router weight decay, and `run_progress` therefore match the 4K run. A changed context requires an explicit `--qk-mult`, applied to all attention layers; `--capacity-factor` overrides the expert receiver capacity.

Harrier now shuffles blocks of 2^20 tokens (`io_block_size = 2**20 // seq_len`), which equals the existing 256-sequence block at 4K. At a longer context the outer block permutation stays the same, so only each cell's in-progress 512-block window reorders. With the previous sequence-sized blocks, a 16K relaunch would have re-read an estimated 2.85T already-seen tokens of the remaining ~9T. At 16K the past main-mixture boundary moves from step 108000 to 108096, and a continuation must pass `--accept-mixture-boundary-shift`.

Canonical hero eval stays at 4K packing, so the inherited `eval_dropless/*` series remains comparable, and the first-step eval now also runs after a checkpoint resume. Per-example FLOPs rise with context, so a FLOPs baseline (`--flops-baseline-step`, `--flops-baseline-total`) keeps `throughput/total_gflops` continuous across the handoff. `trigger_hero.sh` records the context, QK multiplier, capacity, eval context, FLOPs baseline, and boundary acceptance in the W&B lineage and the #8506 launch record. `launch_diagnostics` gains `--optimizer-tokens-per-step`, `--gate-router-weight-decay`, `--eval-seq-len`, and `--eval-prefix`, so a one-rack rehearsal can use the hero's optimizer settings and report long-context eval separately.

The live run is unchanged. A switch still needs a GPU rehearsal from the handoff checkpoint and agreed trial thresholds; see the inventory and validation plan in #9615.
